hero.title: Are you emotionally dependent on your partner?
hero.description: 20 honest questions to find out whether you love your partner or cling to them. Instant result, detailed analysis and concrete next steps.
hero.subtitle: Free, confidential, instant result

section1.title: Emotional dependency is not “loving too much”
section1.intro: The two get confused all the time, and the confusion suits everyone. “I'm like this because I love you too much” sounds better than the truth.
section1.p1: Loving means wanting the other person's presence. Depending means being unable to bear their absence. The nuance looks thin on paper and changes everything in real life: in the first case, your partner adds something to a life that already stands on its own. In the second, they have become the load-bearing wall, and you spend your days watching to make sure it doesn't move.
section1.p2: Emotional dependency is not a medical diagnosis, and it isn't proof of love either. It's a way of functioning: needing the other person in order to feel that you exist, fear of abandonment as the compass for every decision, the gradual erasing of who you were before.
section1.p3: What makes it hard to spot in yourself is that it looks deceptively like the first months of a passion. Except passion settles down and leaves a relationship behind it. Dependency settles in, and it grows precisely where your personal life retreats.
section1.quote: “You cannot be happy as a couple if you don't know how to exist alone.”

section2.title: Loving deeply or depending: the table that helps you decide
section2.intro: The same behaviour can be tender or worrying depending on what drives it. This table compares the two versions, situation by situation.
section2.row1Level: You notice, your day carries on
section2.row1Analysis: Anxiety climbs, you send message after message
section2.row2Level: You miss them a bit, it does you good too
section2.row2Analysis: It's an ordeal, you count the hours
section2.row3Analysis: You give in: conflict feels like a breakup risk
section2.row4Level: Their social life doesn't threaten you
section2.row4Analysis: Every outing without you wakes the fear of being replaced
section2.row5Level: It also exists outside the couple
section2.row5Analysis: It depends entirely on how they look at you

section3.title: The signs that should alert you
section3.p1: No single sign is enough to talk about emotional dependency. Everyone has reread a message three times or taken a silence badly. It's accumulation and repetition that should alert you: when these reactions become your default mode.
section3.p2: Three families of signs come up in most people concerned:
section3.sub1P1: Knotted stomach when they don't reply, insomnia when they pull away, physical relief when the phone finally vibrates. Emotional dependency lives in the body first, before the thoughts. If your partner's absence triggers symptoms close to withdrawal, that's no longer tenderness, it's a signal.
section3.sub2P1: The friends you no longer see, the passion abandoned “for lack of time”, the personal projects postponed. The shrinking happens gently, choice after choice, and you only measure it looking back: what is left in your life that doesn't involve your partner?
section3.sub3P1: You don't say what bothers you, you accept what hurts you, you test their love by provoking crises. Behind these three behaviours, the same engine: the conviction that expressing a need or setting a limit could drive the other person away. When the fear of losing someone steers your choices, the relationship is already off balance.

section4.title: Where does emotional dependency come from?
section4.p1: Nobody chooses to become emotionally dependent. The psychiatrist John Bowlby's work on attachment, extended by Mary Ainsworth's experiments, showed that the way we love as adults is built very early: a child whose attachment figures were unpredictable (present one day, absent the next) learns that love can vanish at any moment, and that it must be watched.
section4.p2: As an adult, the same reflex replays in the couple: hypervigilance at the slightest sign of distance, constant need for reassurance, panic at the idea of abandonment. This is what we call anxious attachment, and knowing your attachment style often sheds sudden light on years of misunderstood reactions.
section4.p3: Childhood doesn't explain everything. Fragile self-esteem, a brutal breakup that never healed properly or a previous toxic relationship can install the same reflexes in someone who didn't have them. Emotional dependency is a learned mechanism, and that is excellent news: what has been learned can be unlearned.
section4.tip: Recognising yourself in these lines is not a verdict. Attachment style is not a permanent box: researchers speak of “earned security” to describe anxious people who became secure, through experience or through work on themselves.

section5.title: What dependency does to your relationship
section5.intro: The cruel paradox of emotional dependency: it damages precisely the relationship it is trying to protect.
section5.pillar1Text: Endlessly reassuring someone whom nothing reassures is a full-time job. Even the most loving partner ends up wearing down, then pulling away, exactly what the dependency dreaded.
section5.pillar2Text: When your whole life rests on one person, every colleague, friend and notification becomes a potential threat. If jealousy is taking up all the room in your daily life, it is rarely acting alone.
section5.pillar3Text: Desire needs a space between two distinct people. In permanent fusion there is no other left to desire, no missing, no surprise. Many fused couples discover this bitterly.
section5.pillar4Text: Whoever is more afraid of losing the other accepts everything, and whoever knows they are indispensable obtains everything. Neither wanted it, but the power imbalance is there, and it opens the door to controlling relationships.

section6.title: Getting out: where you start
section6.p1: Emotional dependency is not a life sentence, but you don't get out by willpower alone, and certainly not by repeating “I need to be less clingy”. Here are the steps that come up in most successful journeys.
section6.sub1P1: This may be the step you're taking right now. Putting the right word on the mechanism changes the question: it's no longer “why do I love them too much?” but “why am I so afraid of losing them?”. The second one has answers.
section6.sub2P1: An activity of yours, friends of yours, a project of yours. Not to make the other person jealous, not to “take some distance”, but to rebuild what existed before: a life that stands without a crutch. Start small: one evening a week is enough to restart the machine.
section6.sub3Title: 3. Sit with the discomfort instead of fleeing it
section6.sub3P1: Not sending the third message. Letting the silence exist without filling it. Saying “this doesn't work for me” and enduring the minutes that follow. Every time you cross the anxiety without giving in to the reflex, you teach your alarm system that it is ringing for nothing.
section6.sub4P1: When the fear of abandonment is old and deep, a psychologist or therapist is the most effective shortcut, and cognitive behavioural therapies in particular are well documented on this subject. Understanding the mechanics of emotional dependency also helps you move forward between sessions.

section7.title: Emotional dependency or dependent personality: don't mix everything up
section7.p1: A point of honesty, because everything gets mixed up on this subject online. The emotional dependency this page talks about is a widespread relational pattern, not an illness. It causes suffering, it can be worked on, but it cannot be diagnosed.
section7.p2: There also exists, in psychiatric classifications such as the DSM-5, a dependent personality disorder: a pervasive need to be taken care of that touches every sphere of life, not just the couple, and which belongs to mental health professionals.
section7.p3: If your dependency extends far beyond your romantic relationship, if it comes with intense distress, dark thoughts or an inability to function day to day, an online test is no longer what you need: talk to your doctor or a psychologist. There is no shame in it: it is actually the strongest decision on this list.
section7.quote: “The goal is not to need nobody. It is to choose someone freely, rather than clinging to them out of fear.”

section8.title: How this test works
section8.p1: Twenty concrete situations, four possible reactions each time, from the most autonomous to the most dependent. No trick questions, no right answers: the test measures the frequency and intensity of your anxious reflexes as a couple, on the registers where dependency really shows: the body, decisions, limits, the fear of emptiness.
section8.p2: Your score places you on four levels, from solid emotional autonomy to dependency that hurts, each with an analysis and tailored next steps. Answer with what you actually do, not with what you would like to do: the test is only worth as much as your honesty.
section8.tip: This test is a self-observation tool, not a diagnosis. No online questionnaire replaces the opinion of a mental health professional. If your answers worry you, that is who you should turn to.

seo.faq1A: No, and this is the most common misconception. Love chooses the other person's presence; dependency cannot bear their absence. You can love deeply while remaining autonomous, and you can be totally dependent on someone you no longer really love: it's the withdrawal that holds you, not the feeling.
seo.faq2Q: Can you overcome emotional dependency on your own?
seo.faq2A: For milder forms, yes: reinvesting in your personal life, learning to tolerate the discomfort of silence and rebuilding your self-esteem are often enough. When the fear of abandonment is old and intense, psychological support speeds things up enormously, especially cognitive behavioural therapies.
seo.faq3A: No. Emotional dependency isn't a medical diagnosis in the first place: it's a relational pattern. This test helps you objectify it and put words on it, but only a mental health professional can assess an individual situation, especially if the suffering is intense.
seo.faq4Q: Why do I get attached so quickly?
seo.faq4A: Fast, intense attachment is often the signature of an anxious attachment style, built early in life: when you have learned that love can disappear, you grab onto it the moment it appears. Fragile self-esteem amplifies the phenomenon, because the other person becomes the proof that you are worth something.
seo.faq5Q: My partner is emotionally dependent: what should I do?
seo.faq5A: Neither reject them nor carry everything. Reassure on the fundamentals (the attachment), not on every crisis, concretely encourage their personal life (friends, activities, projects) and hold your limits with steadiness and kindness. If nothing moves, suggest professional support: your role is not to cure, it is to support.
seo.faq6A: Of course, and far more than people say. Men often live it less visibly (fewer verbal requests for reassurance, more control or jealousy) and seek help later. The underlying mechanism, fear of abandonment and self-worth conditioned on the other's gaze, is exactly the same.
